claims.text: A machine-learning surrogate can be trained on a sparse set of static ab initio free-energy calculations.
The static training calculations can account faithfully for phonon-based vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and simplified electron–vibration coupling.
The proposed surrogate can predict fusion properties of both solid and liquid phases with fidelity similar to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed workflow will have significantly lower computational cost than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The intended domain comprises elemental, binary, and eventually multicomponent high-entropy systems in solid and liquid states near fusion.
The surrogate will interpolate solid- and liquid-phase free energies without full molecular-dynamics trajectories.
The method should be demonstrated on elemental and binary systems before being extended to multicomponent high-entropy systems.
TOR-TILD slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
A learned free-energy surface can simultaneously represent vibrational, anharmonic, and electronic contributions in both solid and liquid phases.
Learning a free-energy landscape from limited high-fidelity static calculations enables interpolation of all significant entropy contributions.
Free-energy interpolation reduces the need for costly ab initio molecular dynamics.
Prior alloy studies have successfully used ab initio-informed learned or surrogate models to extend predictions over composition space.
Configurational entropy can drive high-temperature phase transitions.
Fusion temperatures and solid–liquid free-energy differences will deviate by no more than about 5% from explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results.
The workflow will reduce computational time by approximately an order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The workflow will be significantly faster than TOR-TILD for multicomponent systems.
Explicit ab initio workflows for high-temperature multicomponent alloys are computationally demanding.
The surrogate is expected to remain valid only where entropy and anharmonic effects lie within its calibrated composition and temperature domain.
Strongly nonlinear or extreme anharmonic behavior may require additional calibration because static corrections may not capture all dynamic effects.
A decisive benchmark can compare predicted phase free energies, vibrational entropy, fusion temperature, and computational cost against explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD.
